lessons.title: Potential Is Distance Traveled, Not Starting Point
lessons.key_idea: We misjudge potential by focusing on early talent, when what matters most is how far someone can grow.

lessons.title: Character Skills Beat Natural Talent
lessons.key_idea: Learnable character skills like proactivity, discipline and determination drive growth more than innate ability does.

lessons.title: Become a Creature of Discomfort
lessons.key_idea: Real learning happens when you seek out awkward situations and use new skills before you feel ready.

lessons.title: Be a Sponge, Not a Rock
lessons.key_idea: Growth depends on actively absorbing knowledge, and asking for advice works better than asking for feedback.

lessons.title: Chase Excellence, Not Perfection
lessons.key_idea: Perfectionism slows growth, so aim for high standards while accepting flaws and mistakes along the way.

lessons.title: Turn Practice Into Play and Detours
lessons.key_idea: Make practice enjoyable and see setbacks as detours, because sometimes going backward is how you move forward.

lessons.title: Build Systems That Lift Everyone
lessons.key_idea: Schools, teams and hiring processes can unlock hidden potential by giving everyone the chance to grow.

plan.title: Hidden Potential
plan.author: Adam Grant
plan.confidence_note: I know the book's structure and core arguments well, but I am less certain of some individual stories, so lessons should stick to its central ideas and its best-known examples.
plan.one_liner: Your potential isn't where you start. It's how far you can travel, with the right habits and support.
plan.summary: Adam Grant argues that we put too much weight on natural talent and too little on how people grow. Hidden potential, he says, is not about where you begin but how far you travel. The book has three parts. First come character skills, such as proactivity, discipline and determination, which help us learn. These include getting comfortable with discomfort, soaking up useful knowledge and feedback, and aiming for excellence instead of perfection. Next come structures that keep motivation alive, like turning practice into play and finding new paths when progress stalls. Finally, Grant looks at systems that unlock potential in groups, including schools, teams and hiring processes that spot people who are overlooked. Throughout, he shows that ordinary people can achieve extraordinary things when they have the right habits and the right support around them.
